transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-07
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), James (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood Solutions), Aisha (NovaFinance CTO), Ravi (Head of ML), Lena (Eng Manager), Tom (SRE)

Summary:
Quick Optimize product walkthrough focused on batching and KV/prefix caching recommendations. Discussed NovaFinance constraints (p95 latency targets ~200ms, strict data residency + KMS, cost target for inference). Went through cost model examples and rough hit-rate expectations. Agreed next steps: send cost model sheet, run benchmark, share security docs.

Topics:
- Current infra and pain points
- Batching strategies and latency tradeoffs
- KV/prefix cache behavior and hit-rate tuning
- Cost model walk-through with sample numbers
- Security/compliance checklist for Private deployment

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to run through Redwood Optimize recommendations for batching and prefix/KV cache, keep it practical, we'll show numbers and a sample cost model, feel free to interrupt.
[00:18] Aisha: Thanks, Maya. Quick context - we are trying to move some of our conversational flows off our homegrown inference cluster to reduce ops burden and cost. Our p95 latency target is about 200 milliseconds, and we do strict residency for EU/US markets. Also SOC2 is mandatory for any vendor.
[00:36] Maya: Absolutely, will cover that. James, quick intro?
[00:40] James: Hi all, James Li, I'm the SE focusing on runtime and Optimize. We'll walk through batching knobs, cache profiles, and the model of how these translate to cost.
[00:50] Ravi: Quick Q - our average request is about 150 tokens in and we generate roughly 200 tokens out on average, but there's a long tail of longer sessions for some customers.
[01:05] James: Great, that token distribution is what drives batching efficiency. Two quick rules: batching reduces per-token compute by filling GPU work but adds head-of-line latency; cache (prefix/KV) reduces repeated decoder compute for multi-turn sessions.
[01:22] Lena: Can you define prefix vs KV cache again? We use some internal jargon.
[01:26] James: Sure - prefix cache is essentially storing the encoded prefix (embedding/KV state) so you don't recompute the same context tokens for identical or highly similar prompts. KV cache is the transformer key/value cache across decoding steps to avoid re-encoding previously computed tokens; in Redwood we expose configs to evict by session TTL or total memory.
[01:44] Tom: Are those caches per-tenant? We need isolation.
[01:47] Maya: We support tenant-isolated KV and prefix cache on Dedicated and Private deployments; you can also configure TTLs and explicit invalidation. For hosted we can provide logical separation and retention controls, plus audit logs.
[02:02] Aisha: Ok - show us the numbers you hinted at.
[02:06] James: Yup - quick example from a sample workload similar to yours. Baseline: no cache, minimal batching (batch size ~1-2), 350ms average decode p95 on a T4-equivalent serving VM for this model size - cost X. If we enable moderate batching (batch target 8, adaptive latency cap 80ms) we saw throughput uplift 3x and cost per token drop ~55%, with p95 rising to ~260ms in that config.
[02:36] Ravi: That p95 is above our target. Can batching be combined with priority routing or fast lanes?
[02:40] James: Yes - Redwood supports routing policies. Typical pattern: latency-sensitive routes go to a low-batch fast pool (dedicated or higher-tier instance) and cost-sensitive traffic uses high-batch pools. The platform supports automatic fallback when fast pool capacity is exhausted.
[02:55] Maya: Also worth noting, you can set per-route SLOs and Redwood will aim to keep tail latency within those constraints by selecting proper batch windows.
[03:05] Lena: And caching - what sort of hit rates should we expect for multi-turn banking prompts?
[03:10] James: We looked at similar customers - for structured financial chat, if the conversational state reuses the same account context and prompts, prefix/KV cache hit rates often land between 40%-65% depending on session length and prompt variability. For templated prompts (e.g., balance inquiry, transaction history) hit rates can be >70%.
[03:29] Ravi: So 50% hit means half the tokens are effectively free from decode cost?
[03:33] James: Roughly - if a token is served entirely from cache (i.e., no decoder steps), you avoid the bulk of decoder compute. In practice, partial hits happen: you still pay for attention over the cached keys or have to fetch KVs. We model it conservatively as 30%-50% token compute reduction per cache hit.
[03:50] Maya: I'll pull up a simple cost model on the shared deck - this is the spreadsheet we'll send.
[03:55] [screen share noise]
[04:05] James: Example line: 1M requests, average 350 tokens/request (in+out), baseline compute 350M tokens. With 50% KV hit rate and batching that yields 55% cost reduction, the combined effect can reduce effective compute by ~75% in some workloads - so you might go from 350M to ~90M charged compute units in our model. Caveat: actual savings depend heavily on hit distribution and your batching latency cap.
[04:35] Aisha: Are you modeling network egress or just GPU time?
[04:39] James: The sheet models GPU compute and instance time; we add a line for networking and storage overhead. We'll send the full breakdown.
[04:47] Ravi: How does sequence length variability affect batching? We have many short requests and some with 2k token long tails.
[04:54] James: Redwood's runtime uses sequence-length aware kernels and dynamic batching. You can set max sequence length per pool to avoid long-tail requests blocking short ones. Also, KV/prefix cache helps by absorbing repeated prefixes so long tails are less frequent in the decode stage.
[05:10] Tom: On security - KMS integration and audit logs are must-haves. Can you explain how keys are managed for Private vs Hosted?
[05:18] Maya: For Private, customers can bring their own KMS/HSM and Redwood will integrate to ensure model checkpoints and logs are encrypted under customer keys. For hosted, we support customer-managed keys in partner clouds or Redwood-managed keys with strict ACLs; audit logs are available for all tiers. We'll attach the SOC2 and KMS integration docs.
[05:36] Aisha: Any compliance differences if we go Dedicated vs Private?
[05:40] Priya: Dedicated offers tenant-isolated pools with dedicated GPUs and network controls; Private is the full VPC/control-plane with air-gapped or on-prem options and deeper integration for compliance teams.
[05:53] Ravi: Back to numbers - can you run a benchmark against our model and dataset? We want to validate p95 at our traffic mix and see real hit rates.
[05:58] James: Absolutely. Typical pilot: we ingest a sample traffic trace, spin up a small dedicated pool or a private evaluation cluster, run a 50k-200k request workload with your tokens distribution and measure hit rates and tail latency. We usually instrument trace-level KV hits so you can see where cache helps.
[06:18] Lena: What about warm-up? If we start with an empty cache, initial performance will be worse. Any recommended warm-up strategy?
[06:24] James: Yes - warm-up is important. Two approaches: synthetic warmup that replays past sessions to populate prefix cache, or progressive rollout where you route a subset of traffic through caches and gradually increase. We can provide a replay tool for that.
[06:36] Ravi: Pricing questions - what's the pricing model for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[06:40] Maya: Hosted is usage-based (per-token + per-embedding with tiered discounts). Dedicated is reserved capacity - monthly commit for a pool of GPUs with predictable throughput. Private has a licensing fee plus support. The cost model we'll send maps these to your expected token volumes and projected savings from caching + batching.
[06:57] Aisha: Competitors - we've also looked at Vertex and a self-hosted Mistral stack. How are you different on ops?
[07:03] Maya: We focus on production-grade runtime and an opinionated Optimize toolkit - built-in batching/caching, smart routing across pools, and transparent cost/latency dashboards. We also provide rollout primitives to reduce risk in switching.
[07:18] Ravi: Any limitations with model types - we use a mix of Llama-family and a few closed-source models.
[07:24] James: Redwood supports a broad model catalog and custom model onboarding; for closed-source models we can serve compatible variants and provide quantization profiles. For some exotic ops we might need kernel work but that's part of the model onboarding process.
[07:40] Maya: Ok let's walk through a quick sample config in the sheet - I'll narrate.
[07:44] [shared sheet reading]
[07:50] Maya: Route A: latency-sensitive, pool fast-1, batch target 2, latency cap 50ms, preferred model variant small-quantized. Route B: cost-sensitive, pool cost-1, batch target 16, adaptive window up to 120ms. Both pools have KV cache enabled with TTL 30m and max memory 50GB per node.
[08:12] Lena: If we set TTL 30m, do we risk serving stale context? We need explicit invalidation for some flows.
[08:18] James: You can do explicit invalidation via API call or event-driven invalidation on customer side; also we support sticky session keys to scope caches to sessions.
[08:28] Tom: Any rough infrastructure footprint for the pools? How many gpus for 10k qps?
[08:33] James: It depends on model choice - as a rough thumb: for a 1.5B-ish model optimized on A100-class instance, 1 GPU can do roughly X qps at batch 8 for short sequences; we'll produce exact sizing in the spreadsheet after we run your traces.
[08:50] Ravi: Can you break down the cost math? I want the formula.
[08:53] James: Sure. Core formula in the sheet: Effective_compute_tokens = total_tokens * (1 - cache_effective_fraction) * batching_factor. Where cache_effective_fraction is empirical hit_rate * per_hit_compute_reduction. batching_factor is fraction of compute saved due to batching kernel efficiency (e.g., 0.45 means 55% reduction). Then instance_hours = Effective_compute_tokens / tokens_per_instance_hour. Then cost = instance_hours * instance_hour_cost + network + storage. We'll send the exact cell formulas.
[09:24] Aisha: If we do a pilot, who owns the benchmark infra cost?
[09:27] Maya: For pilot we usually cost-share - Redwood covers some infra and we ask customers to cover cloud GPU hours if using customer's cloud; if we run in Redwood sandbox, Redwood covers most. We can talk specifics for NovaFinance in the SOW.
[09:39] Lena: Any fragile failure modes with caching? Like cache blowups or TTL storms?
[09:44] James: Yes - unbounded cache growth is a concern; we recommend capped memory per pool and eviction policies (LRU, TTL). Also monitor miss spikes after rolls or model updates; Redwood Optimize includes alerts for cache-miss regressions.
[10:00] Maya: Alright, quick recap and next steps?
[10:03] Maya: Action items - Maya will send the cost model, James will schedule the benchmark, Aisha will share traces. We'll aim to reconvene after benchmark results.
[10:12] Aisha: Sounds good, thanks everyone.

Notes on transcript quality: Automated transcription had a few mis-attributed lines and occasional word substitutions (e.g., 'cache hit yields' transcribed as 'cash hits yields'). We'll attach the raw audio for SE review.

References shared: link to cost model spreadsheet (placeholder: https://redwood.app/sheets/nuva-cost-model), SOC2 + security checklist (link), sample benchmark run template (link).
